title: Species profiles: are the intermediates right?
summary: Mole fractions of reactants, products and radicals against time in a constant-volume reactor, in the same panel on a linear and on a log axis. The log panel is where the radicals and intermediates become visible.

media.alt: Two panels of mole fraction against log time for H2, O2, H2O, OH and HO2, the left linear, the right with a logarithmic y axis.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Are intermediates right?
read_the_figure.axes: x: time in ms on a log axis (1e-2 to about 5 ms). y: mole fraction X_i, dimensionless: left panel linear (0 to 0.3), right panel logarithmic (1e-7 to 1).
look_at: When does the major species (H2, O2) start to fall and when does water level off?
Which radicals peak, and when? (OH and HO2 here.)
How many orders of magnitude separate the major species from the radicals?
Are both panels the same run: same T0, p, composition?
read_the_figure.proves: If the model's profiles of reactants, products and intermediates agree with a measurement or with another mechanism in both panels, the chemical pathway, not just the end state or the ignition time, is reproduced.
if_wrong: A radical peak at the wrong time or height in the log panel: the chain-branching steps are wrong even if the ignition time matches.
Final values that do not match: equilibrium thermodynamics or missing products.
Panels with different conditions: the comparison between them means nothing.

terms.meaning: Moles of a species divided by total moles; the fractions sum to one.
A species with an unpaired electron (H, O, OH, HO2) that carries the chain reaction; small in amount, large in effect.
A species made and consumed on the way from reactants to products; it peaks and then falls.
A closed vessel in which density is fixed while the mixture reacts.
Same data on a logarithmic y axis to show species that differ by many orders of magnitude.

remember: Sum of mole fractions = 1 at every time.
Reactants fall, products rise, intermediates peak and fall.
Linear panel for the majors, log panel for the radicals; show both.
T0, p and composition must be stated, and equal in both panels.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x encodes time (log scale), on y the mole fraction. Colour and line style identify the species; the two panels repeat the same lines so the reader can see the majors on the left and the trace species on the right. The footer states the reactor and initial state.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Reacting mixtures contain species with concentrations that differ by six orders of magnitude, and kinetics lives in the small ones. A single linear axis shows only the fuel-to-water transition, a single log axis hides the sharpness of the consumption. Two panels from the same data answer two different questions: how far has the reaction gone, and what are the radicals doing.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: When does the reaction happen? On the time axis the H2 and O2 curves start falling near 0.1 ms and are finished by about 1 ms, with the water curve rising to about 0.28 over the same time. Q2: Which radical peaks first? HO2 peaks near 0.2 ms at about 2e-4, then OH peaks near 0.35 ms at about 6e-3; read on the log panel. Q3: How far apart are the radicals and the fuel? Initially the fuel is 0.30 and OH is near 1e-7, a ratio of about 3e6, so six to seven decades; in the linear panel OH is invisible.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Log y option, same T, p stated: the figure offers the log panel, the footer says T0 = 1100 K, p = 1 atm for both panels, so the reader may compare them. Each is needed: without the log panel the intermediates are invisible, without the common conditions the panels cannot be read together.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: On a log axis a species that changes from 1e-7 to 6e-3 looks as important as the fuel; its absolute contribution is tiny. Different time axes across panels can hide an offset, and a log time axis compresses the late equilibrium stage into a flat line that looks uneventful. Profiles do not show rates: matching profiles can be produced by different reactions.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot normalised profiles (X_i over its maximum) to compare timing, or a pairwise parity plot of peak values. Sensitivity of the profile to each reaction (F9.6) tells why profiles differ; a pathway diagram (F9.8) shows how.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a vertical line at the time of maximum OH, mark the ignition delay on both panels, and overlay measured points with error bars.

steps.title: Mole fraction from mass fractions
steps.note: Mass fractions Y_i and molar masses W_i; check that the X_i sum to one.

steps.title: Decades between two species
steps.note: Counts how many gridlines the log panel needs.

worked.title: Stoichiometric H2-air as mass fractions
worked.problem: Mixture: X(H2) = 0.2958, X(O2) = 0.1479, X(N2) = 0.5563. Find the mass fraction of H2 (W = 2.016, 31.998 and 28.014 g/mol).
worked.answer: Y(H2) is about 2.85 percent, although X(H2) is almost 30 percent: hydrogen is light.

analyze.q: The OH peak in the log panel is 1e4 times lower than the water level. Does it matter that it is small?
analyze.hint: Think about its role in the chain reaction.

analyze.q: Why would the peak of HO2 come before the OH peak?
analyze.hint: What is the order of the chain steps?

evaluate.q: A measured OH profile agrees with the model in height but peaks 0.1 ms earlier. Is the mechanism validated?
evaluate.hint: Both timing and height are features of the pathway.

create: Add a third panel with the mixture temperature and the pressure, sharing the time axis.
Plot the same species against progress variable (water fraction) instead of time. What changes?

checks.q: Why show the same data in two panels?
checks.hint: Which species can you see in each?
checks.answer: The linear panel shows the main reactants and products, the log panel makes the trace radicals visible.

checks.q: X(OH) goes from 1e-7 to 6e-3. How many decades is that?
Water reaches 0.28 but the fuel does not go to zero. Why?
checks.hint: Equilibrium and dissociation at high temperature.
checks.answer: At the reactor's final temperature the reaction is limited by equilibrium: some H2 and O2 remain and radicals persist.
